en.title: Sociology: the whole course
en.short: What sociology is, how a sociology degree is organised, its main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Sociology is the systematic study of society and social life. It asks how social structures, institutions, groups and everyday interactions shape what people do, and how people in turn reproduce or change those structures. It is a social science, so it combines theory with evidence: concepts such as class, status, role, norm, institution and power are defined, then examined against observation. Sociology is not social work, though the two often meet in policy and community practice, and it is not psychology: its main focus is on social relations and organisation rather than individual mental processes. A sociological question often begins by making the familiar strange. Why does a practice that seems natural vary between societies, or change over time? Answering that requires comparison, history and data.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BSc Sociology is commonly a four-year full-time university degree, with accreditation and benchmark requirements set nationally; some programmes are longer where a foundation or part-time route is involved. In the United Kingdom, a BA or BSc in Sociology is usually three years full-time, and a taught MSc is usually one year full-time. In South Africa, a BA or Bachelor of Social Science in Sociology is commonly three years, followed by an honours year and then a master’s. Master’s programmes usually combine advanced theory and methods with a dissertation. Names such as BA, BSc, MA and MSc do not always signal the same content, so read the modules, not only the title.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics build the base. You start with the sociological perspective and the discipline itself, then culture, norms and values; socialisation and the self; social interaction, groups and organisations; stratification, class and mobility; deviance, crime and social control; family and kinship; religion and society; the founders of sociological theory; and the foundations of research.

Core topics apply and deepen this base. Modern theory covers functionalism, conflict theory and interactionism. Contemporary theory follows. Then come the sociology of education; work and economic life; political sociology and the state; urban sociology and urbanisation; demography and population; gender and society; race, ethnicity and minority relations; health, illness and medicine; development, globalisation and global inequality; social movements and social change; quantitative methods and data analysis; qualitative methods; African sociology and postcolonial thought; and social policy, welfare and the state.

Master’s topics raise the level of abstraction and independent work: advanced social theory, especially structure, agency and practice; advanced research design and the dissertation; digital society, technology and platforms; and comparative and historical sociology.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study sociology by linking three things: theory, evidence and your own society. For each concept, write a definition in your own words, then one example from your country and one from elsewhere. Do not collect examples without saying what they show.

Read theory actively. For a theorist, identify the central question, the key concepts, the level of analysis and the main criticism. Compare theories on the same issue, such as inequality or education, rather than learning them as separate summaries.

Treat methods as practical. Learn what each method can and cannot show, and practise a small piece of analysis. In quantitative work, check how variables are coded and what a table actually reports. In qualitative work, keep notes on sampling, access and ethics. Use your library’s databases, and record every source fully so that referencing is easy.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include treating sociology as opinion. A claim about society needs a concept, evidence and a stated limit. Students also confuse a theory with a fact, or present one school of thought as the whole discipline.

Another mistake is to use everyday words as if they were technical terms. Class, culture, gender, race and deviance have ordinary meanings, but sociological definitions are more precise and are often contested.

Many students describe a study without saying how it was designed, or quote a statistic without its date, country and definition. Others compare countries as if their categories were identical. In essays, avoid long description with no argument. State the question, define terms, set out the evidence, consider an objection, and conclude. Finally, do not ignore theory in methods courses, or methods in theory courses; the two belong together.

keyPoints: Sociology studies how social structures and interactions shape action, and how action in turn changes society.
Theory and evidence must be used together; a sociological claim needs a concept, evidence and a stated limit.
Degree length and award names vary by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn each theory by its central question, key concepts, level of analysis and main criticism.
Methods determine what a study can show; do not separate methods from theory.
Define terms precisely and give every statistic its date, country and definition.

en.title: The Sociological Perspective and the Discipline of Sociology
en.short: Sociology’s perspective, the sociological imagination, origins, neighbouring fields and levels of analysis.

sections.heading: What sociology studies
sections.text: Sociology is the systematic study of society and social life. It asks how groups, institutions and social relationships shape what people think and do. Its central habit is the sociological perspective: looking beyond individual motives to the social context. Sociologists study patterns, not only single cases. A social institution is an established way of meeting a need, such as education or the family. Sociology asks how institutions vary and whom they serve.

sections.heading: Sociological imagination
sections.text:
C. Wright Mills called the sociological imagination the ability to link personal troubles to public issues. A trouble is private and felt by one person. An issue is public and shared by many people in a society.

Amina, a graduate in Kano, Nigeria, cannot find work. As her own problem it is a personal trouble. If many graduates in her region face the same gap between schooling and jobs, it becomes a public issue about the economy and education. The sociological imagination moves between the two without blaming the individual alone.

sections.heading: Origins and neighbours
sections.text: Sociology took shape in nineteenth-century industrial Europe, especially Britain, France and Germany. Industrialisation, urban growth and political upheaval made old arrangements uncertain, and scholars began to study society with its own methods. It shares ground with other social sciences. Anthropology often studied small communities and culture, while sociology focused on industrial societies, though the division is blurred. Economics studies markets and production; sociology studies the social relations around economic life. Psychology studies the individual mind; sociology studies groups and social structure. Political science studies government and power; sociology studies power across the whole society.

sections.heading: Levels of analysis
sections.text: Micro sociology studies face-to-face interaction, such as a job interview. Meso sociology studies organisations and communities, such as a school or town. Macro sociology studies large institutions, class structures, states and global systems. The levels connect: a national job shortage is macro, a factory’s hiring policy is meso, and an interview is micro.

keyPoints: Sociology studies how social relationships, institutions and groups shape human life.
The sociological imagination links personal troubles to public issues.
Sociology grew in nineteenth-century industrial Europe as societies changed rapidly.
Sociology overlaps with anthropology, economics, psychology and political science but keeps a focus on social patterns.
Micro analysis studies face-to-face interaction, meso analysis organisations and communities, and macro analysis large institutions and global structures.

en.title: Culture, Norms and Values
en.short: The components of culture, ethnocentrism and relativism, subcultures and cultural change.

sections.heading: Components of culture
sections.text: Culture is the learned, shared way of life of a society. Its components include symbols, anything to which people give shared meaning, such as a flag or a word; language, a system of symbols used for communication; values, shared ideas about what is good and desirable; norms, rules that guide behaviour; sanctions, rewards or punishments that enforce norms; and material culture, the physical objects people make and use, from tools to clothing. The ideas and symbols are called non-material culture.

sections.heading: Norms and sanctions
sections.text: Norms vary in strength. Folkways are everyday customs, such as greeting a lecturer. Mores are strong moral rules, such as honesty in examinations. Laws are formal norms enforced by the state. Sanctions may be positive or negative, formal or informal. Praise is an informal positive sanction; a fine is a formal negative one. In many universities, including in Nigeria, queuing is a folkway, while cheating is a more and also a formal rule with penalties.

sections.heading: Ethnocentrism and relativism
sections.text: Ethnocentrism judges another culture by the standards of one’s own and often assumes that one’s own is superior. Cultural relativism tries to understand a culture in its own terms. It is a method of study, not automatic approval of every practice. A visitor who sees a local greeting custom may call it strange. Ethnocentrism stops there; relativism asks what the greeting means to the people who use it.

sections.heading: Subcultures and change
sections.text: A subculture shares distinct norms and values within a larger culture, such as a campus religious society or a professional group. A counterculture rejects or opposes central norms, for example a movement that rejects consumerism. Culture is learned through socialisation, shared by members, and changed by invention, discovery, diffusion and conflict. A Ghanaian student may learn campus slang, carry it home, and change the speech of friends.

keyPoints: Culture includes symbols, language, values, norms, sanctions and material culture.
Norms are rules of behaviour; sanctions are the rewards and punishments that support them.
Folkways are everyday customs, mores are strong moral rules, and laws are formal state-enforced norms.
Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one’s own standards, while cultural relativism studies them in their own terms.
Subcultures share distinct norms within a larger culture, and countercultures oppose central norms.
Culture is learned, shared and changed through invention, discovery, diffusion and conflict.

en.title: Socialisation and the Development of the Self
en.short: Nature and nurture, Cooley, Mead, Freud, Piaget, agents of socialisation and resocialisation.

sections.heading: Nature and nurture
sections.text: Human development is neither purely biological nor purely social. Biology gives capacities such as language learning and temperament. Social experience turns these capacities into particular skills, beliefs and selves. Cases of children raised with little human contact show that severe isolation damages language and social development, but such cases are rare and cannot be used as clean experiments. Sociologists therefore study how nurture works through socialisation, the lifelong process of learning norms, values and roles.

sections.heading: Theories of the self
sections.text: Charles Cooley (1902) described the looking-glass self: we imagine how we appear to others, imagine their judgement, and feel pride or shame. The self is thus built from imagined reactions. George Herbert Mead went further. The self has two sides: the 'I', the spontaneous response, and the 'me', the internalised attitudes of others. Children learn role taking, the ability to see themselves from another person’s point of view, through imitation, play and organised games. In games they must hold several roles at once and follow rules, which builds the generalised other, the sense of society’s expectations. Sigmund Freud argued that the superego internalises parental and social rules through early conflict, though his claims are disputed. Jean Piaget showed that children think in stages, from sensorimotor action to formal abstract reasoning, so socialisation must fit their cognitive level.

sections.heading: Agents of socialisation
sections.text: Agents of socialisation are the people and institutions that teach us. The family is the first agent, teaching language, trust and basic values. Schools teach formal knowledge, punctuality and universal rules. Peer groups teach loyalty, style and independence from adults. Mass media and social media shape images of success and normality. Religion teaches meaning, morality and ritual. These agents may agree or conflict.

sections.heading: Resocialisation
sections.text: Resocialisation is learning new norms and roles that replace or reshape earlier ones. It happens at university, in migration, in prison or in religious conversion. For example, Amina moves from a close family in Kano to a Lagos university. She keeps some home values while learning new study habits, dress codes and friendships.

keyPoints: Socialisation is the lifelong process through which people learn norms, values and roles.
Biology provides capacities, but social experience shapes how they develop.
Cooley’s looking-glass self says we build self-image from how we imagine others see us.
Mead distinguished the spontaneous 'I' from the social 'me' and linked role taking to the generalised other.
Freud and Piaget linked the self to early emotional conflict and to stages of cognitive development.
Family, school, peers, media and religion are agents of socialisation, and resocialisation reshapes roles across life.

en.title: Social Interaction, Groups and Organisations
en.short: Status, roles, group types, bureaucracy, dramaturgy and ethnomethodology in everyday interaction.

sections.heading: Status and roles
sections.text: Social interaction rests on shared expectations. A status is a social position, such as student or cashier. An ascribed status comes from birth or circumstance, for example ethnicity. An achieved status is earned or chosen, such as a degree. Each status carries roles, the expected behaviour attached to it. Role conflict arises when two different roles make clashing demands: a student who also works nights may be needed in class and at work at once. Role strain arises within one role: a nurse must comfort a patient and still finish a ward round. People manage both by prioritising or negotiating.

sections.heading: Groups
sections.text: Primary groups are small, intimate and lasting, such as family or close friends; members know one another as whole persons. Secondary groups are larger, more impersonal and goal-directed, such as a lecture class or workplace team. An in-group is a group we belong to and feel loyal towards; an out-group is one we do not belong to. A reference group is a group we use as a standard for judging ourselves, even without belonging to it. A first-year student may compare her marks with a study group she admires.

sections.heading: Organisations
sections.text: Formal organisations are deliberately planned to achieve goals through rules and offices. Max Weber described bureaucracy as an ideal type with hierarchy, written rules, impersonal offices, salaried officials and records. It can be efficient and fair, but also rigid. In a Nigerian university, registration may pass through several offices; rules make it predictable, yet delays frustrate students.

sections.heading: Interaction as performance
sections.text: Goffman’s dramaturgical model compares social life to theatre. People perform on a front stage, managing impressions for an audience, and relax back stage. Ethnomethodology, linked to Harold Garfinkel, studies how people create order in everyday talk and action. Breaching experiments deliberately break small rules to reveal this work. Social order is thus produced in each encounter, not only imposed by structures.

keyPoints: Statuses are social positions; ascribed statuses are given by birth or circumstance, while achieved statuses are earned or chosen.
Role conflict is tension between two different roles, while role strain is tension within one role.
Primary groups are intimate and lasting; secondary groups are larger, impersonal and goal-directed.
In-groups are groups we belong to, out-groups are groups we do not belong to, and reference groups are standards for self-judgement.
Weber’s bureaucracy is an ideal type marked by hierarchy, written rules, impersonal offices and records.
Goffman’s dramaturgical model treats interaction as performance, and ethnomethodology studies how people produce everyday order.

en.title: Social Stratification, Class and Mobility
en.short: Slavery, caste, estate and class; Marx, Weber, functionalism and conflict; measuring class; mobility types.

sections.heading: Systems of stratification
sections.text: Stratification is the ranking of people into groups with unequal access to income, power and respect. Slavery treats people as property, as in the Atlantic slave trade. Caste is closed and ascribed: a person is born into it and marries within it, as in Hindu India. Estate belonged to feudal Europe, where law fixed clergy, nobility and commoners. Class is open in principle and rests mainly on economic position.

sections.heading: Marx and Weber
sections.text:
Karl Marx divided modern society by relation to the means of production. Owners form the bourgeoisie; wage workers form the proletariat. Profit comes from unpaid labour, or surplus value. A class in itself shares a position; a class for itself is conscious and organised.

Max Weber kept class but added two dimensions. Class is a market situation, similar chances to earn. Status is the honour a group receives, shown in lifestyle. Party is organised power. The three can diverge: a teacher may hold status but little income.

sections.heading: Explaining inequality
sections.text: Functionalism, in Davis and Moore’s 1945 essay, holds that some roles need rare talent and long training, so unequal rewards are needed to fill them. Melvin Tumin (1953) replied that this cannot explain inherited wealth, and that reward does not match importance. Conflict theory, following Marx and Weber, holds that stratification serves those already holding power.

sections.heading: Measuring class and mobility
sections.text:
Class is usually measured by occupation, as in the UK’s National Statistics Socio-economic Classification, or by income and education. Schemes differ by country; check the current source.

Mobility is movement between positions. Vertical mobility is up or down; horizontal is sideways between similar ranks. Intergenerational mobility compares parents and children; intragenerational mobility happens within one life. Absolute mobility is the raw rate; relative mobility, or social fluidity, compares chances once the job structure is allowed for.

Case: Ngozi’s father farms near Enugu; she trains as a nurse. That is intergenerational upward mobility, helped by structural change as nursing jobs grew.

keyPoints: Stratification systems differ in openness: slavery and caste are ascribed, estate is fixed by law, class is open in principle.
Marx defines class by relation to the means of production and treats profit as unpaid labour.
Weber adds status and party to class, and the three dimensions can point in different directions.
Functionalism justifies unequal rewards by scarcity of talent and long training; conflict theory sees them as serving existing power.
Class is measured mainly by occupation, income, wealth and education, and the schemes used vary by country.
Vertical, horizontal, intergenerational and intragenerational mobility are distinct, and relative mobility is not the same as absolute mobility.

en.title: Deviance, Crime and Social Control
en.short: Defining deviance and crime, Durkheim, Merton, labelling, learning and control theories, and crime statistics.

sections.heading: Deviance and crime
sections.text:
Deviance is behaviour that breaks a social norm. Crime is behaviour that breaks the criminal law and can be punished by the state. Not all deviance is crime. Norms vary between societies and over time, so the same act may be deviant in one place and accepted in another.

Social control is how groups keep people to norms. Informal control works through family, friends, gossip and shame. Formal control works through police, courts and prisons.

sections.heading: Durkheim and Merton
sections.text:
Émile Durkheim argued that deviance is normal and can be functional. It affirms shared norms when people condemn it, strengthens solidarity, and can open the way to change. He used anomie for normlessness, when shared rules weaken.

Robert Merton’s strain theory starts from a gap between cultural goals, such as money success, and the legitimate means available. People adapt by conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism or rebellion. Innovation uses illegitimate means for approved goals.

sections.heading: Learning, labelling, control
sections.text:
Sutherland’s differential association says criminal behaviour is learned through interaction in intimate groups. They learn techniques and motives.

Labelling theory says deviance is not only the act but the reaction to it. A label can become a self-fulfilling identity, and powerful groups do more labelling. Hirschi’s control theory asks why most people conform. Social bonds hold them: attachment, commitment, involvement and belief. Crime is more likely when these bonds are weak.

sections.heading: Statistics and a case
sections.text:
Official crime statistics are not a simple record of crime. They show only crimes known to police and recorded by them. Many crimes are not reported or recorded, the dark figure. Reporting and recording vary with police priorities, victim trust and legal change.

Case: In Lagos, Nigeria, a school leaver without paid work joins a group that resells stolen phones. Strain explains the pressure, differential association the learning, labelling the record that closes doors, and weak bonds the drift.

keyPoints: Deviance breaks social norms; crime breaks criminal law and is punishable by the state.
Durkheim saw deviance as normal and functional, and used anomie for normlessness.
Merton’s strain theory links crime to a gap between goals and legitimate means.
Labelling theory treats deviance as a reaction and a self-fulfilling identity.
Differential association says criminal behaviour is learned in intimate groups; control theory says weak bonds free people to offend.
Official crime statistics suffer from under-reporting and recording bias, so they are not a full measure of crime.

en.title: Family, Marriage and Kinship
en.short: Family types, descent and residence rules, marriage forms, bridewealth and forces that change family life.

sections.heading: Family forms and functions
sections.text:
A family is a group related by blood, marriage or adoption; a household shares a dwelling, and the two differ. The nuclear family is two parents and their dependent children. The extended family adds other kin, often three generations, and is common across Africa. A single-parent family has one parent with children, after divorce, death or by choice.

Murdock listed sexual, reproductive, economic and educational functions; Parsons stressed primary socialisation and stabilising adult personalities. Schools, churches and employers now share these tasks.

sections.heading: Descent and residence
sections.text:
Descent rules decide which kin group a person belongs to. Patrilineal descent traces through men, matrilineal through women, bilateral through both. The Akan of Ghana are matrilineal: a child belongs to the mother’s abusua, and inheritance follows that line. The Yoruba of Nigeria trace descent mainly through men.

Residence rules decide where a couple lives: patrilocal with the husband’s people, matrilocal with the wife’s, neolocal in a new home. Urban wage work makes neolocal residence more common.

sections.heading: Marriage and bridewealth
sections.text:
Monogamy is marriage to one spouse at a time. Polygyny is one husband with several wives, permitted in many African customary and Islamic systems. Polyandry, one wife with several husbands, is rare. In levirate marriage a widow is expected to marry her late husband’s brother.

Bridewealth is a transfer from the groom’s family to the bride’s; dowry moves the other way. Example: bridewealth agreed at ₦500,000 plus two goats at ₦40,000 each gives ₦580,000, paid in three instalments.

sections.heading: What changes family life
sections.text:
Industrialisation moved paid work out of the home and encouraged smaller, neolocal households. Migration splits households: a parent works in a city or abroad while children stay with grandparents, common in West and Southern Africa. Religion shapes marriage rules; Islamic law permits up to four wives.

Law changes family life directly. South Africa’s Recognition of Customary Marriages Act 120 of 1998 gave customary wives equal status. Ghana’s Intestate Succession Law 1985 (PNDCL 111) gave widows and children fixed shares. Kenya’s Marriage Act 2014 recognised five marriage systems and set 18 as the minimum age.

keyPoints: A household and a family are not the same; households may contain people who are not kin.
Descent rules (patrilineal, matrilineal, bilateral) decide group membership and inheritance.
Bridewealth passes from the groom’s family to the bride’s; dowry passes from the bride’s side.
Polygyny is permitted in many African customary and Islamic systems; polyandry is rare.
Industrialisation, migration, religion and law have reshaped family forms, sometimes against custom.
Murdock’s claim that the nuclear family is universal is criticised by studies of matrilineal societies.

en.title: Religion, Belief and Society
en.short: Durkheim, Weber and Marx on religion, religious organisations, secularisation and religion’s vitality in Africa.

sections.heading: Classical approaches
sections.text:
Durkheim divided the world into the sacred, set apart and forbidden, and the profane, ordinary life. In The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912) he argued that rituals create collective effervescence, a shared excitement, and that society worships itself through religion.

Weber’s Protestant Ethic (1905) linked Calvinist predestination to capitalism. Calvinists sought signs of salvation in disciplined work. Worldly asceticism, hard work without enjoyment, helped produce rational capitalism.

Marx called religion the opium of the people. It comforts the oppressed but can dull the will to change unjust conditions.

sections.heading: Organising religion
sections.text:
Ernst Troeltsch distinguished church and sect. A church is large, established and inclusive, often tied to the state. A sect is smaller, exclusive and in tension with wider society, demanding strong commitment.

H. Richard Niebuhr added the denomination, a stable and respectable body that tolerates other faiths. The term cult is used for a loose, novel group with low commitment, but it is pejorative; sociologists prefer new religious movement.

sections.heading: Secularisation debate
sections.text:
Secularisation means the declining social significance of religion. Bryan Wilson and Steve Bruce argued that rationalisation, science and pluralism weaken religion, especially in Western Europe. Church attendance there has fallen.

But the thesis is uneven. Religion remains strong in the United States and the global South, and new forms appear. Peter Berger, once a supporter, later argued that religion persists and that secularisation is not universal.

sections.heading: Religion in Africa
sections.text:
Religion remains central in many African societies. Christianity and Islam grow, and Pentecostal churches and African independent churches shape politics, health, education and family life.

A Lagos neighbourhood may have a Pentecostal church running a school and a mosque running a clinic; both offer identity and welfare where state welfare is limited. Such vitality challenges the secularisation thesis, though scholars disagree on how far it will last.

keyPoints: Durkheim: religion separates the sacred from the profane and binds society through ritual.
Weber: the Protestant ethic of disciplined work helped create rational capitalism.
Marx: religion is the opium of the people, a comfort that can mask injustice.
Troeltsch’s church is established and inclusive; a sect is exclusive and in tension with society.
A denomination is a stable, respectable body; 'cult' is pejorative, so scholars say new religious movement.
Secularisation is uneven: Western Europe has declined, but religion remains vital in Africa and elsewhere.

en.title: The Founders of Sociological Theory
en.short: Comte, Spencer, Martineau, Marx, Durkheim, Weber, Simmel and Du Bois on order, conflict, meaning and modernity.

sections.heading: Order and progress
sections.text:
Auguste Comte coined the term sociology and argued that society should be studied positively, through observation and comparison. His law of three stages says thought moves from theological, to metaphysical, to positive. He stressed order and progress.

Herbert Spencer used an organic analogy: society is like a body whose parts differentiate and integrate. He saw evolution moving toward industrial, individualist societies. Harriet Martineau translated Comte, wrote How to Observe Morals and Manners (1838), an early guide to method, and studied institutions and everyday manners.

sections.heading: Conflict and race
sections.text:
Karl Marx asked how capitalism shapes conflict. He argued that the mode of production, the way goods are made, creates classes: owners of capital (bourgeoisie) and wage workers (proletariat). Workers experience alienation, estrangement from their labour and product. Class struggle drives historical change.

W. E. B. Du Bois placed race beside class. In The Philadelphia Negro (1899) he used surveys and interviews. He named the colour line, the racial divide, and double consciousness, seeing oneself through other eyes. A Lagos factory worker, Ngozi, may sell her labour yet feel the product belongs to another; a migrant may also face exclusion.

sections.heading: Social facts
sections.text:
Émile Durkheim treated social facts as external constraints on individuals, such as laws and shared beliefs. He asked what holds society together.

Mechanical solidarity binds simple societies through shared likeness; organic solidarity binds modern ones through interdependence from the division of labour. Rapid change can produce anomie, normlessness. His study of suicide showed that social integration and regulation affect personal acts.

sections.heading: Meaning and modernity
sections.text:
Max Weber argued that sociology should interpret social action through verstehen, empathetic understanding. Ideal types are analytical models, not real groups. He traced rationalisation, the spread of calculation and rules, and warned of an iron cage.

Georg Simmel studied social forms such as the dyad, triad and stranger. He saw money and city life intensify individual freedom and cultural distance. These founders set later agendas: order, conflict, meaning and modernity.

keyPoints: Comte coined sociology and promoted positivism, order and progress.
Spencer compared society to an organism and stressed evolution and differentiation.
Martineau translated Comte and wrote an early guide to sociological method.
Marx analysed class conflict, alienation and capitalism; Du Bois added race, the colour line and double consciousness.
Durkheim defined social facts and explained solidarity and anomie.
Weber used verstehen and ideal types and traced rationalisation; Simmel studied social forms and modernity.

en.title: Foundations of Sociological Research
en.short: Concepts, variables, hypotheses, reliability, validity, quantitative and qualitative strategies, data sources, ethics.

sections.heading: Concepts and variables
sections.text: Research begins with concepts, which are abstract ideas such as social class or stress. A variable is a concept made measurable, because it can take different values. Operationalisation is the step of saying exactly how a variable will be measured, for example a stress score from a ten-item questionnaire. A hypothesis is a testable statement about a relationship between variables, such as: students who sleep less than six hours report higher stress than those who sleep longer. It must be open to being shown false.

sections.heading: Reliability and validity
sections.text: Reliability means consistency. A measure is reliable if it gives similar results when repeated or when used by different researchers. Validity means the measure really captures the concept it claims to measure. A scale may be reliable but invalid if it consistently measures tiredness rather than stress. Good research aims for both, and it reports its limits honestly.

sections.heading: Strategies and data
sections.text: Quantitative strategies collect numbers and look for patterns across many cases, often using surveys or official statistics. Qualitative strategies collect words, images or observations and explore meaning in fewer cases, often using interviews or fieldwork. Neither is automatically better; the question decides. Data may be primary, collected by the researcher, or secondary, already collected by others. Main sources include surveys, interviews, observation, documents and official statistics.

sections.heading: Ethics of research
sections.text: Ethical rules protect people who take part. Informed consent means telling participants the purpose, procedures, risks and their right to withdraw, then obtaining voluntary agreement. Anonymity means the researcher cannot link data to a person. Confidentiality means the researcher can identify a person but promises not to disclose that identity. Doing no harm means avoiding physical, psychological or social injury, and weighing benefits against risks. Codes differ by country and professional body, so check the current local rules. A Nigerian researcher studying campus stress should get consent, keep names out of reports, and offer support if a participant becomes distressed.

keyPoints: A concept becomes a variable when it is defined in a way that can be measured.
A hypothesis is a testable statement about a relationship between variables.
Reliability is consistency; validity is measuring what the concept claims to measure.
Quantitative strategies use numbers and large cases; qualitative strategies use meaning and fewer cases.
Primary data are collected by the researcher; secondary data already exist.
Informed consent, anonymity, confidentiality and doing no harm are basic ethical safeguards, but local codes vary.

en.title: Modern Sociological Theory: Functionalism, Conflict and Interactionism
en.short: Functionalism, conflict theory, interactionism, exchange theory and rational choice, compared through one case.

sections.heading: Functionalism
sections.text: Structural functionalism treats society as a system of interdependent parts. Talcott Parsons argued that institutions such as family, school and religion meet needs that keep the system going. Robert Merton refined this: manifest functions are the intended, recognised consequences of an institution; latent functions are unintended and unrecognised. He added dysfunctions, consequences that weaken the system. Its strength is that it explains order and integration. Critics say it is conservative, assumes shared values and explains change poorly.

sections.heading: Conflict theory
sections.text: Conflict theory sees society as held together by power, not agreement. Groups struggle over scarce resources, and institutions serve dominant interests. Karl Marx’s class analysis is the classic version; later conflict theorists study authority, status and other inequalities. Its strength is that it takes power, inequality and change seriously. Critics reply that it overstates conflict, underplays cooperation and shared norms, and can reduce everything to interest.

sections.heading: Interactionism and exchange
sections.text: Symbolic interactionism studies how people create meaning in face-to-face interaction. George Herbert Mead traced the self to social interaction; Herbert Blumer argued that people act toward things on the basis of meaning, and meanings are revised through interpretation. Its strength is everyday life and identity; its weakness is that it can neglect large structures. Exchange theory, associated with George Homans and Peter Blau, treats interaction as a trade of rewards and costs. Rational choice theory, associated with James Coleman, says actors choose the action with the highest expected utility under constraints. Both give clear mechanisms, but critics say they assume too much calculation and ignore norms, emotion and power.

sections.heading: One fact, four readings
sections.text: Take a first-year university lecture. Functionalism asks what it does for the system: it transmits knowledge and socialises students. Conflict theory asks who benefits: it reproduces class advantage through credentials. Symbolic interactionism asks how meanings are negotiated: lecturer and students perform roles and interpret cues. Exchange and rational choice ask what actors weigh: students compare fees, time and expected earnings. Each theory highlights something the others miss.

keyPoints: Structural functionalism explains how institutions meet system needs and maintain order.
Merton distinguishes manifest functions, which are intended, from latent functions, which are unintended.
Conflict theory explains institutions as products of power and inequality and as sources of change.
Symbolic interactionism explains how meanings and the self are produced in face-to-face interaction.
Exchange theory and rational choice explain action as a calculation of rewards, costs and expected utility.
Each theory answers a different question about the same social fact, so they can complement rather than simply contradict one another.

en.title: Contemporary Social Theory: Structure, Difference and Agency
en.short: Structuralism, feminism, postmodernism and the structure-agency debate.

sections.heading: Structuralism
sections.text: Structuralism looks for hidden systems beneath surface events. From Saussure’s linguistics it takes the idea that meaning comes from differences within a language, not from things themselves. Lévi-Strauss applied this to kinship and myth; Althusser to Marx’s social formation. It revises Durkheim and Marx by treating social relations as a deep grammar. Post-structuralism accepts the focus on language but denies fixed structures. Derrida shows meanings deferred; Foucault studies power and discourse, not a single centre. This revises classical theory by questioning universal reason and progress.

sections.heading: Feminist theory
sections.text: Feminist theory revises the classical canon for its male-centred categories. Liberal feminism seeks equal rights and opportunities within existing institutions. Radical feminism names patriarchy, a system of male dominance, as the root problem and links the personal to the political. Black feminism, with intersectionality from Kimberlé Crenshaw, argues that race, class and gender combine; it criticises white feminism’s single focus. Postcolonial feminism, associated with Chandra Mohanty and Gayatri Spivak, asks how colonialism and Western feminism represent Third World women. These strands disagree about reform versus deep change.

sections.heading: Postmodern and late modern
sections.text: Postmodern theory distrusts grand narratives. Lyotard defines the postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives, the large stories of progress or emancipation. It revises classical sociology by denying that one theory can capture society. Late-modern theory is less sceptical. Giddens, Beck and Bauman describe a modernity that has become reflexive: people must monitor and choose their lives under global risks. They keep classical questions about order and change but reject simple determinism.

sections.heading: Structure and agency
sections.text: The structure and agency debate asks whether social life is shaped by external systems or by purposeful actors. Giddens’s structuration says structures are both medium and outcome of action. Bourdieu’s habitus, durable dispositions acquired through socialization, links the two. Archer’s morphogenesis separates them analytically. Case: Amaka, a trader in Enugu, faces credit rules and gender expectations, yet negotiates prices and joins a savings group. Her action reproduces or alters those structures.

keyPoints: Structuralism seeks deep systems; post-structuralism denies fixed centres and stable meaning.
Liberal feminism pursues equal rights; radical feminism targets patriarchy; black and postcolonial feminism stress intersectional and colonial power.
Postmodern theory rejects grand narratives; late-modern theory keeps a reflexive modernity.
Giddens’s structuration and Bourdieu’s habitus link structure and agency; Archer separates them.
These currents revise classical theory by questioning universal reason, male-centred categories and simple determinism.

en.title: Sociology of Education: Schooling, Inequality and Mobility
en.short: Functions of schooling, reproduction and mobility, hidden curriculum, Bernstein, Bourdieu and credential inflation.

sections.heading: Functions and sorting
sections.text:
Education transmits knowledge and skills, socialises young people into shared values, and sorts them for work. Functionalists stress these contributions to order and the economy.

Conflict theorists reply that schooling also reproduces class relations by teaching obedience and by awarding credentials that favour advantaged groups. Education is meant to promote mobility, but sorting can limit it. Schooling can both open and close opportunities.

sections.heading: Hidden curriculum and codes
sections.text:
The hidden curriculum is what pupils learn from school organisation rather than the official syllabus: punctuality, deference to authority, competition and compliance. Basil Bernstein argued that schools favour an elaborated code, with explicit, context-independent language, over a restricted code, which relies on shared context.

Neither code is inferior, but mismatch can disadvantage pupils whose homes use the restricted code more. Language of instruction matters in multilingual African countries: early schooling in a familiar language can support learning, while a later switch to a colonial language can create barriers.

sections.heading: Cultural capital
sections.text:
Pierre Bourdieu argued that cultural capital, the knowledge, manners, tastes and credentials valued by schools, is unevenly distributed and converted into educational success. It takes embodied, objectified and institutionalised forms: personal dispositions, cultural goods such as books, and qualifications. Schools appear neutral but reward the culture of dominant groups, so advantage is reproduced.

A concrete case: Amina, trader’s daughter in Nigeria, speaks her home language well but attends a school where lessons and exams are in English. Chidi, from a professional family, has English books and educated relatives at home. Scholarships and mother-tongue teaching can widen mobility.

sections.heading: Credential inflation
sections.text:
Credential inflation occurs when jobs demand higher qualifications than the tasks require, so students seek more certificates to stand out. This raises costs and can deepen inequality.

In many African systems, examinations inherited from colonial rule and scarce public university places have long made certificates gatekeepers. Policy responses include quality basic education, relevant vocational training and fair financing, but each involves trade-offs.

keyPoints: Education transmits knowledge, socialises and sorts people, but it can both reproduce and reduce inequality.
The hidden curriculum teaches values and behaviour through school routines rather than the official syllabus.
Bernstein’s elaborated and restricted codes describe language styles; schools tend to favour elaborated code.
Bourdieu’s cultural capital is valued knowledge and credentials that schools reward, helping reproduce advantage.
Credential inflation raises qualification demands and can increase costs and inequality.
In multilingual African systems, language of instruction and exam language can shape access and achievement.

en.title: Sociology of Work and Economic Life
en.short: Classical division of labour, alienation, Taylorism, Fordism, post-Fordism, informal work and precarious work.

sections.heading: Classical accounts of labour
sections.text: Adam Smith (1776) argued that the division of labour raises productivity. In his pin factory example, splitting tasks let a small group make thousands of pins a day. He warned that repetitive tasks could dull workers. Émile Durkheim (1893) treated the division of labour as a source of social solidarity, not only wealth: interdependence makes people need one another. Karl Marx (1844) saw alienation under capitalism. Workers are estranged from the product they make, the act of making it, their human potential and other workers.

sections.heading: Taylorism and Fordism
sections.text: Frederick Winslow Taylor’s scientific management (1911), or Taylorism, separated planning from doing. Managers timed motions and set quotas, while workers followed instructions. Fordism built on this with the moving assembly line, standardised mass production and mass consumption. Henry Ford’s plants paid relatively high wages so workers might buy cars. Post-Fordism describes the shift from the 1970s towards flexible production, smaller batches, information technology and service work. It can mean more autonomy for some, but also short contracts and insecurity for many.

sections.heading: Informal and precarious work
sections.text: The informal economy is work that is unregistered and outside labour law. Keith Hart used the term informal sector in a study of Ghana in the early 1970s. A market trader in Accra who keeps no accounts and pays no tax is a common example. Precarious work is paid work with low security, low pay and few rights, such as casual or temporary contracts. Unemployment means being without work while available and actively seeking a job. Underemployment and discouraged workers who have stopped searching are related measures, but discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed.

sections.heading: Work and identity
sections.text: Work gives people identity, daily routine and social ties. It also places them in a class structure through occupation and income. Gender shapes work: women are concentrated in some occupations and do more unpaid care, while men dominate others. A Nigerian example: a female bank teller and a male mechanic may both work full time, but their jobs carry different pay, status and security.

keyPoints: Smith argued that the division of labour raises productivity but can dull workers.
Durkheim saw the division of labour as creating organic solidarity through interdependence.
Marx described alienation as separation from the product, the work process, human potential and other workers.
Taylorism separated planning from doing, and Fordism combined assembly-line production with mass consumption.
Post-Fordism brings flexible production but often insecure and short-term work.
Work shapes identity, class and gender through occupation, pay and occupational segregation.

en.title: Political Sociology and the State
en.short: Theories of the state, power and authority, citizenship, civil society and clientelism in Africa.

sections.heading: Theories of the state
sections.text: A state is a set of institutions ruling a territory and enforcing decisions. Max Weber defined it by its claim to a monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force. Pluralists, such as Robert Dahl, see the state as an arena where competing groups press claims and no single group always wins. Elite theorists, from Mosca and Pareto to C. Wright Mills, argue that a small group holds decisive power. Marxists tie the state to class rule: instrumentalists call it a tool of capitalists, while structuralists say it must reproduce capitalism even without direct orders. Weberians stress bureaucracy, law and legitimacy.

sections.heading: Power, authority, citizenship
sections.text: Power is the capacity to achieve aims even against resistance. Authority is power accepted as legitimate. Weber distinguished traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority. Citizenship is membership of a state with rights and duties. T. H. Marshall described civil, political and social rights, but his account came from Britain and rights vary by country. A nation is a community claiming common identity, often imagined through language, history and education; nation and state do not always coincide.

sections.heading: Civil society and clientelism
sections.text: Civil society means associations between household and state: unions, churches, clubs, professional bodies and NGOs. It can check state power, but it can also be divided or captured. Clientelism is the exchange of material benefits for political support, often through brokers. In parts of Africa, colonial legacies, personal rule and weak administrative reach have blended formal bureaucracy with patronage, sometimes called neopatrimonialism. This varies widely: Botswana and Somalia are not usefully described in the same terms.

sections.heading: States and societies
sections.text: States shape society through law, taxation, schools and categories such as citizenship. Societies shape states by resisting, negotiating and staffing them. Suppose a Lagos ward officer controls stall permits. Traders obey rules but ask a broker to speed up permits for a fee. This is bargaining, not domination. Michael Mann’s infrastructural power, the capacity to reach into society, helps explain why some states implement policies and others do not.

keyPoints: Weber defined the state by its claim to a monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force in a territory.
Pluralists see the state as an arena of competing groups; elite theorists see a small group holding decisive power.
Marxists disagree over whether the state is an instrument of capitalists or a structural requirement of capitalism.
Authority is legitimate power, while citizenship is state membership with rights and duties and nations are claimed communities.
Civil society can check the state but can also be divided or captured by patronage.
Clientelism and neopatrimonialism describe how formal rules and personal patronage mix in some African states, but the pattern varies widely.

en.title: Urban Sociology and Urbanisation
en.short: Chicago ecology, Simmel and Wirth, migration, informal settlements and rapid African urbanisation.

sections.heading: Chicago ecology
sections.text: The Chicago School of the 1920s and 1930s studied the city as a social laboratory. Robert Park, Ernest Burgess and Roderick McKenzie developed urban ecology, the idea that city space is arranged through competition and succession, like plant communities. Burgess’s concentric zone model pictured zones spreading outward from the centre: business district, transition zone, working-class housing, suburbs. Later critics said it described Chicago too neatly and ignored culture, planning and inequality.

sections.heading: Simmel and Wirth
sections.text: Georg Simmel’s essay The Metropolis and Mental Life (1903) argued that city life intensifies nervous stimulation. People respond with reserve, punctuality and blasé indifference, which protect the self but can make relationships instrumental. Louis Wirth’s Urbanism as a Way of Life (1938) linked size, density and heterogeneity to weaker primary ties, greater anonymity and more formal social control. Critics note that city dwellers still form strong networks and that urbanism varies by culture and class.

sections.heading: Migration and informality
sections.text: Rural-urban migration is movement from countryside to city, often for work, education or services. It can be voluntary or forced by land pressure and conflict. Many migrants enter informal settlements: housing built outside planning and building rules, with insecure tenure and limited services. Informal work is common. Urban poverty means inadequate income, shelter, water, sanitation and safety, not merely low income. Consider a family moving to Nairobi or Lagos and renting a room in an unplanned area; their welfare depends on transport, tenure and public services.

sections.heading: African urban challenges
sections.text: Rapid urbanisation in Africa brings opportunities and risks. Cities can create jobs, markets and innovation, but growth that outpaces housing, transport, water and waste services produces congestion, flooding and disease risk. Governments face pressure to upgrade settlements, formalise land and extend services. Policies vary widely by country and city, so students should check current official sources rather than rely on general figures.

keyPoints: The Chicago School used urban ecology and the concentric zone model to explain city space.
Simmel saw the metropolis as intensifying stimulation and encouraging reserve and blasé attitudes.
Wirth linked urban size, density and heterogeneity to anonymity and formal social control.
Rural-urban migration is driven by work, education, services and sometimes land pressure or conflict.
Informal settlements have insecure tenure and limited services, and urban poverty is multidimensional.
Rapid African urbanisation can create opportunity but strains housing, transport, sanitation and governance; policies vary by country and city.

en.title: Demography and Population
en.short: Fertility, mortality, migration, population pyramids, demographic transition, Malthus and population policy.

sections.heading: Measuring population change
sections.text:
Demography studies population size, structure and change. Change equals births minus deaths plus net migration. Fertility is actual childbearing; fecundity is biological capacity. The crude birth rate (CBR) is births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000. Mortality is measured by the crude death rate (CDR). Migration is movement across a boundary; net migration is immigrants minus emigrants.

Worked example: population 10,000; 300 births, 100 deaths, 200 net migrants. CBR = 300 ÷ 10,000 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000. CDR = 100 ÷ 10,000 × 1,000 = 10 per 1,000. Net migration rate = 200 ÷ 10,000 × 1,000 = 20 per 1,000. Growth rate = (300 − 100 + 200) ÷ 10,000 × 1,000 = 40 per 1,000, or 4%.

sections.heading: Age structure and transition
sections.text: Population pyramids plot age groups by sex. A broad base and narrow top suggest high fertility and mortality; a narrow base and wide top suggest ageing. The demographic transition model describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. Death rates usually fall first, birth rates later. Timing varies by country; the model is not a law.

sections.heading: Malthus and policy
sections.text: Thomas Malthus, in An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), argued that population tends to grow geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so checks limit growth. Critics cite technological change, trade, agricultural intensification (Ester Boserup) and the demographic transition. Population policy may be pronatalist (encouraging births) or antinatalist (discouraging births). Family planning, education and health services are common; coercive measures raise rights concerns.

sections.heading: Data and debate
sections.text: Official sources include the United Nations World Population Prospects, the World Bank World Development Indicators, the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and national censuses. The debate on population growth and development is unresolved. Growth is not a simple cause of poverty or prosperity. Outcomes depend on institutions, human capital, women’s education, health, resources and consumption. A favourable age structure can support a demographic dividend, the economic gains from a large working-age population, but only with jobs and policy.

keyPoints: Population change = births − deaths + net migration.
Crude birth rate = births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000; crude death rate uses deaths.
Population pyramids show age and sex structure, and the demographic transition is a model, not a universal law.
Malthus predicted checks on population growth; critics stress technology, trade, agricultural intensification and the transition.
Population policy can be pronatalist or antinatalist, and coercive measures raise rights concerns.
Use UN World Population Prospects, World Bank WDI, DHS and national censuses, and treat population growth and development as conditional, not fixed.

en.title: Gender and Society: Social Construction, Power and Inequality
en.short: Sex versus gender, socialisation, patriarchy, masculinities and inequality in work, school, politics and home.

sections.heading: Sex and gender
sections.text: Sex refers to biological traits such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy. Gender refers to the social meanings, roles, identities and expectations attached to those traits. The distinction matters because many differences between women and men are learned and change across societies. Sex is not always a simple binary; intersex people exist. Sociologists study how gender is produced in everyday life and built into institutions.

sections.heading: Socialisation and labour
sections.text: Gender socialisation is the process through which families, schools, media, religion and peers teach children what is expected of girls and boys. It can be explicit, as when chores are assigned by sex, or subtle, as when praise rewards different behaviour. The gendered division of labour is the allocation of paid work, unpaid domestic work and care by sex. In many societies women do more housework and caregiving, while men are more likely to hold paid jobs and authority. This division is not natural; norms, wages, tax rules and childcare sustain it.

sections.heading: Patriarchy and masculinities
sections.text: Patriarchy is a system of male dominance that operates in families, workplaces, politics and culture. It does not mean every man is powerful; class, race and age shape who benefits. Masculinity refers to socially learned ideals of manhood, such as toughness or being the provider. These ideals can pressure men and justify violence. Feminist critiques differ. Liberal feminists stress equal rights; radical feminists focus on patriarchy and bodily autonomy; socialist feminists link gender inequality to capitalism and unpaid domestic labour; Black and postcolonial feminists show how race, class and colonial history shape gender.

sections.heading: Inequality and a case
sections.text: Gender inequality appears in education, work, politics and the household: girls may face school barriers, women face lower pay and fewer promotions, and women remain under-represented in parliaments. In a hypothetical Nigerian case, Adaeze’s family expects her to fetch water and care for siblings, while Musa gets fees and a quiet room. Later she earns less in informal trade; he gets a salaried job. Household rules, school and work combine.

keyPoints: Sex is biological; gender is social.
Gender socialisation teaches roles through family, school, media and peers.
The gendered division of labour assigns paid work and unpaid care differently by sex.
Patriarchy is institutionalised male dominance, not simply individual men.
Feminist critiques differ in their focus on rights, patriarchy, capitalism and colonial history.
Gender inequality persists in education, work, politics and the household.

en.title: Race, Ethnicity and Minority Relations
en.short: Race as social construction, ethnicity, prejudice, discrimination, assimilation, pluralism and conflict.

sections.heading: Race as construction
sections.text: Race is often treated as biological, but sociology treats it as a social construction. Societies select physical features, give them meaning, and build categories. Boundaries vary between countries and change over time, and genetic variation lies mostly within, not between, socially defined groups. Race still shapes life chances, so it is real in its consequences. Racism ranks people by race.

sections.heading: Ethnicity and tribalism
sections.text: Ethnicity is a shared identity based on culture, language, descent, history or homeland. It is not fixed: boundaries change, and people can belong to more than one category. Tribalism is a contested term. It usually means strong loyalty to one’s ethnic group, often with hostility to outsiders. Many sociologists avoid the word tribe because it can stereotype African societies and make ethnic identity seem ancient. Ethnic loyalty can be mobilised politically, especially when groups compete for state resources.

sections.heading: Prejudice and discrimination
sections.text:
Prejudice is an attitude, a preconceived judgement about a group. Discrimination is unequal treatment. Institutional racism is when an organisation’s rules, routines or policies produce unequal outcomes for a racial or ethnic group, even without deliberate intent.

In a Nigerian university town, Ada, from a minority language group, is told by a landlord that there are no rooms. Later a friend from the majority group is offered one. That is individual discrimination. If the housing office routinely gives majority-group students first choice through an unwritten rule, the pattern is institutional ethnic discrimination.

sections.heading: Models and conflict
sections.text:
Models of majority-minority relations describe how dominant and subordinate groups live together. Assimilation expects minorities to adopt the dominant culture. Pluralism accepts that groups coexist while keeping distinct cultures. Multiculturalism is a state policy that recognises and supports diversity.

Ethnic conflict often arises where ethnic boundaries coincide with unequal access to land, jobs or state power. In Africa, colonial boundaries grouped diverse peoples, and competition for state resources has sometimes been mobilised along ethnic lines. Conflict is not simply ancient hatred; institutions, inequality and leaders shape it.

keyPoints: Race is a social construction: societies give physical differences meaning, and the categories vary across time and place.
Ethnicity is a shared cultural identity, while tribalism is a contested term for strong ethnic loyalty that can turn hostile.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is unequal treatment; institutional racism is unequal outcome produced by organisational rules.
Assimilation expects minorities to adopt the dominant culture, pluralism accepts coexistence, and multiculturalism is a state policy of recognising diversity.
Ethnic conflict is shaped by colonial boundaries, unequal access to resources and political mobilisation, not only by ancient hatred.
Dominant and minority are about power, not simply numbers.

en.title: Sociology of Health, Illness and Medicine
en.short: The social model of health, Parsons’s sick role, medicalisation, inequalities, health systems and stigma.

sections.heading: Health as social
sections.text:
The biomedical model treats illness as a bodily malfunction to be cured. The social model sees health as shaped by social conditions and asks how society defines illness. The World Health Organization (1948) defined health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just absence of disease.

Talcott Parsons (1951) described the sick role: illness is sanctioned deviance. The sick person is excused duties and not blamed, but must want to recover and must seek competent help. Critics say it fits acute illness well and chronic illness badly.

sections.heading: Medicalisation
sections.text: Medicalisation is the process by which a condition or behaviour comes to be defined and treated as a medical problem. Pregnancy, ageing and grief have been medicalised. Irving Zola and Peter Conrad argue this expands professional power and turns social problems into individual ones; others reply that it can bring relief and reduce blame.

sections.heading: Determinants and systems
sections.text:
Social determinants of health are the conditions of birth, growth, work, housing and income that shape health. They help explain inequalities: poorer and less educated people generally fall ill more and die earlier.

Health systems differ. In pluralistic systems people move between clinics, pharmacies, herbalists and faith healers. Traditional medicine is part of public health in some countries and unregulated in others; check national policy.

sections.heading: Illness and stigma
sections.text:
Erving Goffman (1963) defined stigma as an attribute that discredits a person, spoiling normal identity. Stigma can delay diagnosis and treatment.

Case: a young man in a Nigerian town develops tuberculosis. Fearing neighbours will call him cursed, he hides the cough and buys cough syrup at a chemist. Weeks pass before he reaches a clinic. The delay is social, not only medical.

keyPoints: The social model locates the causes of health and illness in social conditions, not only in the body.
Parsons’s sick role exempts the ill person from duties but obliges them to want to recover and to seek help.
Medicalisation means defining a condition or behaviour as a medical problem, which can empower doctors or bring relief.
Social determinants such as income, education, work and housing help explain health inequalities.
Health systems vary: many are pluralistic, mixing biomedicine with traditional and faith healing.
Goffman showed that stigma spoils identity and can delay diagnosis and treatment.

en.title: Development, Globalisation and Global Inequality
en.short: Theories and measures of development, global flows, and effects on work, culture and inequality in Africa.

sections.heading: Theories of development
sections.text: Development means improvement in living standards, capabilities and freedom. Modernisation theory, associated with Rostow, says societies move from traditional to modern through industrialisation, education and stable institutions. Critics call it Eurocentric and blind to colonial power. Dependency theory argues that poorer countries supply cheap raw materials and labour while surplus drains to richer countries, so underdevelopment is produced by the relationship. Wallerstein’s world-systems theory divides the capitalist world-economy into core, semi-periphery and periphery. Countries can move between positions, but the hierarchy persists.

sections.heading: Measuring development
sections.text: Measures of development differ. GDP per capita is total output divided by population, but it ignores distribution and unpaid work. The Human Development Index combines life expectancy, education and income. The Multidimensional Poverty Index counts deprivations in health, education and living standards. The Gini coefficient measures inequality from 0, perfect equality, to 1, total inequality. Purchasing power parity adjusts incomes for price differences. Figures change yearly, so check current UNDP and World Bank reports.

sections.heading: Global flows
sections.text: Globalisation is the interdependence of economies and societies through flows of trade, capital, people and information. Trade moves goods and services; capital moves as investment, loans and remittances; people move as workers, migrants and refugees; information moves through media and the internet. Global value chains split production across countries. Consider Amina, a fictional garment worker in an export processing zone in Kenya. She sews clothes for a European brand. She gains a wage and skills, but her contract is insecure and the brand captures more value.

sections.heading: Effects and debates
sections.text: Effects are uneven. Globalisation creates jobs, export earnings and ideas, but many are precarious, informal and divided by gender. Culture is not homogenised; local people adapt and mix global forms, though power shapes whose culture spreads. Inequality between and within countries can widen when elites and connected regions gain while others are marginalised. Africa’s position is shaped by colonial extraction, commodity dependence, debt and aid. Debates continue over whether globalisation develops or underdevelops the global South.

keyPoints: Modernisation theory sees development as movement from traditional to modern institutions and values, but critics call it Eurocentric.
Dependency theory says core countries drain surplus from the periphery, producing underdevelopment.
World-systems theory divides the capitalist world-economy into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
GDP per capita, HDI, MPI and Gini measure different things; no single measure captures development.
Globalisation flows through trade, capital, people and information, often organised in global value chains.
Globalisation creates jobs and cultural mixing but can deepen inequality and precarious work in the global South.

en.title: Social Movements and Social Change
en.short: Theories of change, movement life cycles and tactics, resource mobilisation, and cases of protest and revolution.

sections.heading: Theories of social change
sections.text: Evolutionary theories treat change as gradual movement from simple to complex societies, as in Auguste Comte and Herbert Spencer. Early versions assumed one path for all societies; later ones allow many. Cyclical theories see rise and fall: Ibn Khaldun linked dynastic rise to asabiyya, group solidarity, and decay to its loss; Vilfredo Pareto described the circulation of elites; Pitirim Sorokin saw cultures alternating between ideational and sensate forms. Conflict theories hold that change comes from struggle over scarce resources. For Karl Marx, class conflict drives history.

sections.heading: Life cycle and tactics
sections.text: Herbert Blumer described movements passing through social unrest, popular excitement, formalisation and institutionalisation. Later writers use emergence, coalescence, bureaucratisation and decline. Tactics range from insider methods such as lobbying, petitions and legal action to outsider methods such as strikes, boycotts, marches, sit-ins and civil disobedience. Charles Tilly called the set of tactics available in a given era its repertoire of contention.

sections.heading: Resources and identity
sections.text: Resource mobilisation theory (McCarthy and Zald, 1977) asks how grievances become organisation: money, members, skills, media access and allies matter more than discontent alone. Political opportunity structure, the openings or closures in the political system, shapes when protest succeeds. New social movement theory (Touraine, Melucci, Habermas, Offe) studies movements of identity and lifestyle, such as environmental, feminist and peace movements, which act on civil society and culture rather than only on the state.

sections.heading: Protest, reform, revolution
sections.text: Protest demands change without seeking power. Reform changes rules within the existing order; revolution transforms the political and social order itself. The anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa combined protest, mass defiance and armed struggle before negotiation brought democracy in 1994. Nigeria’s #EndSARS protests of October 2020 spread from social media to the streets within days, showing how digital tools cut the cost of mobilisation. France’s revolution of 1789 shows rapid, violent transformation of a whole order.

keyPoints: Evolutionary theories see gradual change, cyclical theories see recurrence, and conflict theories see struggle.
Movements typically pass through emergence, coalescence, bureaucratisation and decline.
Tactics range from insider lobbying to outsider protest; Tilly called the available set a repertoire of contention.
Resource mobilisation theory stresses money, members, skills and allies over grievance alone.
New social movement theory focuses on identity, culture and civil society.
Reform changes rules within the existing order; revolution transforms the order itself.

en.title: Quantitative Research Methods and Data Analysis
en.short: Survey design, sampling, measurement, descriptive statistics, association and critical reading of quantitative evidence.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text: Survey design starts with a clear population, the whole group being studied, and a sampling frame, a list from which a sample is drawn. Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection: simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster samples. Non-probability sampling does not: convenience, purposive, quota and snowball samples. Probability samples support estimates of sampling error; non-probability samples cannot. Response rate, mode of interview and pilot testing affect data quality. A pilot is a small trial run of the questionnaire.

sections.heading: Measuring and describing
sections.text: Questionnaire construction turns concepts into variables. Use clear, neutral, single-barrelled questions, and avoid leading wording. Measurement levels are nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio. Reliability means consistency; validity means measuring the intended concept. Descriptive statistics summarise data. The mean is Σx ÷ n; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most frequent. Percentages show composition. In a survey of 100 students, 60 women and 40 men, 30 women and 10 men use the library weekly. Row percentages are 30 ÷ 60 × 100 = 50% for women and 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25% for men. The difference is 25 percentage points.

sections.heading: Association and inference
sections.text: Cross-tabulation compares two categorical variables, usually with row or column percentages. Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear association between two interval or ratio variables; Pearson r runs from −1 to +1. Significance testing asks whether a sample result is unlikely under a null hypothesis of no effect. A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme if the null is true; alpha, often 0.05, is the cut-off. A small p-value is not proof of importance. Check effect size, sample size, missing data and causal claims.

keyPoints: Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; non-probability sampling does not.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; percentage = (part ÷ total) × 100.
Cross-tabulation compares groups using row or column percentages.
Pearson r = covariance(x, y) ÷ (standard deviation of x × standard deviation of y), and it runs from −1 to +1.
A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true.
Significance is not the same as importance; check effect size, sample design and missing data.

en.title: Qualitative Research Methods
en.short: Ethnography, interviews, focus groups, life histories, content analysis, coding, trustworthiness and ethics.

sections.heading: Methods and a case
sections.text:
Ethnography is long-term study of a setting, usually through participant observation: the researcher joins daily life and keeps field notes. In-depth interviews are open conversations that follow the informant’s account. Focus groups usually gather six to ten people so discussion reveals shared norms and disagreements. Life histories record a person’s whole life over several sessions. Content analysis codes documents or media systematically.

A student studying Lagos market credit might observe stalls, interview eight traders and run two focus groups.

sections.heading: Sampling and coding
sections.text:
Qualitative sampling is usually purposive: cases are chosen for what they can teach, not statistical representativeness. Theoretical sampling adds cases until new data stop surprising the analyst. Snowball sampling asks participants to recommend others.

Coding labels segments of data. Open coding names what is happening; focused coding groups labels into themes. Thematic analysis compares themes across cases. If three traders lend only to kin and two lend to neighbours, the theme is conditional trust.

sections.heading: Reflexivity and trust
sections.text:
Reflexivity means examining how the researcher’s age, gender, class or assumptions shape the data. Trustworthiness is the qualitative answer to validity and reliability. It includes credibility, whether findings fit participants’ accounts; transferability, whether readers can apply them elsewhere; dependability, whether the process is documented; and confirmability, whether findings follow from the data.

Triangulation compares methods or sources. Member checking asks participants to comment on draft findings. An audit trail records decisions.

sections.heading: Fieldwork ethics
sections.text:
Fieldwork ethics begins with informed consent: people should know the study’s purpose, what participation involves, and that they may withdraw. Confidentiality protects what is said; anonymity hides who said it.

Researchers must avoid harm, respect privacy and be careful with power. Covert observation needs strong review. Ethics committees and data protection rules differ by country and institution, so check current requirements.

keyPoints: Ethnography studies a setting over time through participant observation and field notes.
In-depth interviews and focus groups reveal accounts and shared norms, while life histories cover a whole life.
Purposive and theoretical sampling choose information-rich cases; coding labels data and thematic analysis groups labels into themes.
Reflexivity examines the researcher’s influence, and trustworthiness covers credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.
Triangulation, member checking and an audit trail strengthen qualitative claims.
Informed consent, confidentiality, anonymity, harm avoidance and attention to power are basic fieldwork ethics; local rules vary.

en.title: African Sociology and Postcolonial Thought
en.short: Colonial roots of African sociology, ubuntu and communalism, postcolonial theory and the postcolonial state.

sections.heading: Colonial origins
sections.text:
Sociology and social anthropology grew in Africa inside colonial institutions: universities and research institutes meant to serve colonial administrators. A. R. Radcliffe-Brown held a chair at Cape Town in the 1920s.

Critics say imported categories distorted what they described. 'Tribe' and 'primitive' pictured African societies as bounded and static. Archie Mafeje argued that 'tribalism' was an ideology, not a description. Akinsola Akiwowo urged theory built from African sources, such as Yoruba oral poetry.
