sections.heading: Communalism and ubuntu
sections.text:
Communalism describes social life in which duties to kin and community weigh heavily and are met through reciprocity rather than through market or state. It is a broad description, not one system.

Ubuntu, an Nguni word, is summed up as 'a person is a person through other persons'. It treats personhood as achieved through relationships, and South African courts invoke it.

Two cautions: communal societies were also hierarchical and patriarchal, so do not romanticise them; and ubuntu is a family of ideas, not one doctrine.

sections.heading: Postcolonial and decolonial theory
sections.text:
Postcolonial theory studies how colonial rule shaped culture, knowledge and identity, and how those effects outlive independence. Frantz Fanon wrote on the psychology of racism and on decolonisation as remaking the self. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) showed Western scholarship producing the 'Orient' it described. Gayatri Spivak asked whether the subaltern can speak; Achille Mbembe analysed power in the postcolony.

Decolonial theory, developed mainly by Latin American scholars, argues that coloniality outlives colonial rule: the racial ordering of knowledge and labour persists. Aníbal Quijano called this the coloniality of power.

sections.heading: The postcolonial state
sections.text: African sociologists asked how the state inherited at independence works. Mahmood Mamdani’s Citizen and Subject (1996) described a bifurcated state: direct rule and civil rights in towns, indirect rule through 'customary' chiefs in the countryside, which he called decentralised despotism. Peter Ekeh (1975) argued that colonialism left two publics, a civic public and a primordial public. Claude Ake questioned whether imported democracy could deliver development.

keyPoints: Sociology in Africa grew inside colonial institutions and often served colonial administration.
Critics argue that imported categories such as 'tribe' distorted African societies; Mafeje called tribalism an ideology rather than a description.
Communalism and ubuntu treat personhood as rooted in relationships, but communal societies were also hierarchical and should not be romanticised.
Postcolonial theory examines how colonial culture and knowledge outlive independence; decolonial theory adds coloniality, the racial ordering that persists.
Mamdani’s bifurcated state combined direct rule and civil rights in towns with indirect rule through customary chiefs in the countryside.
Ekeh’s two publics and Ake’s work on democracy show African scholars building theory about the postcolonial state itself.

en.title: Social Policy, Welfare and the State
en.short: Welfare state models, poverty and social exclusion, social security, and health, education and housing policy.

sections.heading: Welfare state models
sections.text:
A welfare state is a state that takes responsibility for the basic welfare of its people through social policy: collective measures on income, health, education and housing. Gøsta Esping-Andersen (1990) compared welfare states by how far they let people live without selling their labour, which he called decommodification.

He described three ideal types. The liberal type relies on means-tested help and markets, as in the United States. The conservative type preserves status and family roles, as in Germany. The social democratic type offers universal benefits, as in Sweden. Scholars add Mediterranean and East Asian types, but these are ideal types, not fixed boxes.

sections.heading: Poverty and social security
sections.text:
Poverty can be absolute, a lack of basic necessities, or relative, falling far below the usual living standard. Social exclusion is broader: it means being shut out of work, services, networks and political voice.

Social security is the main income-protection tool. It may be contributory insurance, as in Germany; tax-funded and universal; or means-tested assistance. Brazil’s Bolsa Família, a conditional cash transfer, pays poor families who keep children in school and attend health checks. In countries with large informal economies, such as Nigeria and Ghana, contributory schemes cover few workers, so tax-funded or community arrangements matter more.

sections.heading: Health, education and housing
sections.text:
Health, education and housing are mixed economies of welfare, combining state, market and family. Health care may be tax-funded, as in the UK National Health Service; social insurance, as in Germany; or a national scheme, as in Ghana’s National Health Insurance Scheme.

Education is often free at primary level, as in Uganda and Kenya, but enrolment can rise faster than quality. Housing may be state-built, as by Singapore’s Housing and Development Board, or left to private rent and family support. Comparing countries means asking who pays, who receives, and whether benefits reduce dependence on employers and on unpaid family care.

keyPoints: A welfare state takes collective responsibility for income, health, education and housing.
Esping-Andersen’s three ideal types are liberal, conservative and social democratic.
Decommodification measures how far benefits let people live without selling their labour.
Poverty can be absolute or relative; social exclusion adds work, services and voice.
Social security may be contributory, universal or means-tested.
Welfare is a mix of state, market and family, so compare who pays and who receives.

en.title: Advanced Social Theory: Structure, Agency and Practice
en.short: Bourdieu, Giddens, Archer, Habermas, Foucault and critical realism on structure and agency.

sections.heading: Bourdieu: habitus and field
sections.text: Pierre Bourdieu links structure and agency through habitus, field and capital. Habitus is durable dispositions, acquired in socialisation, that shape perception, judgement and action. A field is a structured social space, such as banking, with its own rules and stakes. Capital is resources: economic, cultural, social and symbolic. Practice arises where habitus meets field. Dispositions incline action without determining it, and agents struggle over capital. Amina, a first-generation graduate, enters a bank; her habitus and cultural capital help or hinder her, not fix the outcome.

sections.heading: Giddens and Archer
sections.text: Anthony Giddens’s structuration theory treats structure as both medium and outcome of action: the duality of structure. Structures are rules and resources that people draw on and reproduce, often unintentionally. Margaret Archer’s morphogenesis keeps structure and agency distinct. Structure enables and constrains action; action then elaborates or reproduces structure. Morphogenesis means structural elaboration; morphostasis means reproduction. Archer argues that Giddens conflates the two and explains change poorly.

sections.heading: Habermas and Foucault
sections.text: Jürgen Habermas distinguishes communicative action, oriented to mutual understanding, from strategic action, oriented to success. The lifeworld is the shared background of meanings; systems like markets and states coordinate by money and power. When system logic invades the lifeworld, this is colonisation. Michel Foucault treats power as dispersed and productive, not only repressive. Discourses are systems of statements that constitute objects and subjects. Power and knowledge shape what can be said and done, yet subjects can resist. Foucault reframes the problem as subjectivation rather than structure versus agency.

sections.heading: Critical realism
sections.text: Critical realism, associated with Roy Bhaskar, argues that reality has depth: observable events and underlying mechanisms. Social structures are real generative mechanisms that enable and constrain action without determining it. Agency is transformative, and structures are reproduced or changed through practice. This separates structure and agency analytically without making them independent substances. Each answers differently: Bourdieu via disposition and field, Giddens via duality, Archer via morphogenesis, Habermas via communication and system, Foucault via discourse and power, critical realism via mechanisms.

keyPoints: Bourdieu explains practice as the meeting of habitus and field, with agents competing for capital.
Giddens treats structure as both medium and outcome of action, the duality of structure.
Archer’s morphogenesis separates structure and agency so that structural elaboration can be analysed.
Habermas contrasts communicative action with strategic action and warns of the colonisation of the lifeworld.
Foucault sees power and discourse as productive, shaping subjects who can still resist.
Critical realism treats structures as real generative mechanisms that enable and constrain transformative agency.

en.title: Advanced Research Design and the Dissertation
en.short: Covers epistemologies, mixed and comparative designs, proposals, literature reviews, project management and defence.

sections.heading: Epistemological positions
sections.text: Epistemology is the theory of what knowledge is and how it can be gained. Positivism treats social life as having regularities that can be observed and explained causally, often by testing hypotheses with quantitative data. Interpretivism holds that people act on meanings, so research must understand those meanings from inside, often through qualitative work. Critical realism, associated with Roy Bhaskar, argues that observable events are produced by deeper structures and mechanisms that exist independently of our observations. It asks what mechanisms generate the patterns we see and can combine quantitative and qualitative evidence. These are philosophical positions, not fixed methods.

sections.heading: Mixed and comparative designs
sections.text: A mixed-methods design combines quantitative and qualitative strands in one study. The strands may run in sequence, where one informs the other, or converge, where both are collected and integrated. The justification must be explicit, such as complementarity, triangulation or explanation. A comparative design examines two or more cases selected to control variation. For example, Ada compares why women in two Ghanaian market towns join rotating savings groups. She selects towns with similar trade but different credit access, then interviews members and checks membership records. The comparison helps isolate the condition that matters.

sections.heading: From proposal to defence
sections.text: A proposal states the problem, question, design, ethics and timetable. The literature review should not be a list of summaries; it should show the debate, identify a gap and justify your question. A good research question is focused, answerable with available time and data, and connected to that gap. Manage the project with a written plan, early ethics approval, regular supervision notes and backup copies. For the defence, prepare a short account of what you asked, how you answered it and what limits remain. Anticipate questions about case selection, researcher bias and alternative explanations. Answer calmly and concede weaknesses honestly.

keyPoints: Positivism explains observed regularities; interpretivism understands meaning; critical realism explains underlying mechanisms.
Mixed methods combine quantitative and qualitative strands with a stated purpose.
Comparative designs select cases to control variation and test explanations.
A literature review must identify a gap, not just summarise sources.
A feasible research question fits the time, data and ethical constraints.
A defence explains and limits the claims; honest concessions strengthen credibility.

en.title: Digital Society: Technology, Platforms and Social Change
en.short: Social shaping of technology, platforms, algorithmic control, digital inequality, social media and AI.

sections.heading: Shaping technology
sections.text: Technological determinism says technology drives social change. The social shaping of technology approach rejects this: social choices, power and culture shape how a technology is designed, adopted and used. A tool has affordances, possibilities and limits, but users and institutions decide what those become. A farm in Kaduna, Nigeria may use mobile money differently from a bank in Lagos because trust, fees and network coverage differ. The same device can empower or control depending on who owns the data and rules.

sections.heading: Platforms and algorithms
sections.text: The platform economy is organised around digital platforms that match users, workers and advertisers and take a cut. Ride-hailing, delivery and freelance sites rely on algorithmic control: software assigns tasks, sets prices, tracks performance and can deactivate workers automatically. In a fictional case, Ngozi drives for a Lagos ride-hailing app. The app sets her fare, monitors her route and lowers her rating if passengers complain. She is formally self-employed, yet managed by code. This is a core debate: flexibility versus dependence and weak bargaining power.

sections.heading: Digital inequality
sections.text: Digital inequality is unequal access to, and benefit from, digital technology. Researchers often separate access, skills and outcomes. The digital divide was first seen as a gap between the connected and the unconnected. A second-level divide concerns skills and meaningful use, and a third-level divide concerns whether use improves life chances. A student with a smartphone but no electricity, data or quiet space is still disadvantaged. Gender, income, language, disability and rural location can all matter.

sections.heading: Media, AI and surveillance
sections.text: Social media allow people to present identity and coordinate action. They can support political mobilisation through weak ties, loose connections, and fast sharing. But visibility also invites surveillance, misinformation and unequal attention. Artificial intelligence raises debates about bias, opacity and accountability: a facial recognition system may misread darker faces if trained on narrow data. Surveillance is the monitoring of people and data, now often continuous and commercial. Scholars debate whether these tools expand voice or entrench control.

keyPoints: Technological determinism says technology drives social change; the social shaping approach says social choices and power shape technology.
The platform economy matches users, workers and advertisers, while algorithmic control manages people through data, ratings and automated decisions.
Digital inequality has layers of access, skills and outcomes, so devices alone do not close the divide.
Social media can support identity and protest, but visibility also brings surveillance, misinformation and unequal voice.
Debates on AI and surveillance centre on bias, opacity, accountability and privacy.

en.title: Comparative and Historical Sociology
en.short: Methods of comparison, Mill’s methods, historical sociology and theories of states, revolutions and capitalism.

sections.heading: Comparing cases
sections.text: Comparative sociology explains outcomes by comparing a small number of cases. Case selection is therefore part of the argument. A most similar systems design compares cases that are alike on many features but differ on the outcome. A most different systems design compares cases unlike in background but alike in outcome. Crucial cases test a theory where it is most or least likely to hold. Process tracing follows mechanisms within a case, linking conditions to outcomes over time.

sections.heading: Mill’s methods
sections.text: John Stuart Mill described the method of agreement: cases sharing an outcome may share a cause. The method of difference compares cases alike except for one condition. The method of concomitant variation looks for parallel changes. These methods are guides, not proof, because cases are few and causes interact. Historical sociologists combine them with chronology, archives and secondary histories.

sections.heading: Historical sociology
sections.text: Historical sociology studies social change over time, using sources critically and placing cases in context. It looks for path dependence, where early choices constrain later ones, and critical junctures, moments when alternatives open. It avoids reading the present backwards. A concrete case is Skocpol’s States and Social Revolutions, which compares France, Russia and China. She argues that revolutions arose from state crises under international pressure combined with agrarian class relations that enabled peasant revolt, not from class conflict alone.

sections.heading: States, revolutions, capitalism
sections.text: Classical studies include Tocqueville on democracy and centralisation, Weber on legitimate domination and capitalism, and Moore on agrarian class relations and routes to dictatorship or democracy. Tilly links European state formation to war and extraction; Wallerstein places capitalism in a world-system of core, periphery and semiperiphery. To build explanations, state mechanisms and scope conditions, derive observable implications, compare cases, and test rival accounts. Beware selection bias, equifinality (several paths to one outcome) and Eurocentrism.

keyPoints: Case selection shapes what a comparison can show; most similar and most different designs answer different questions.
Mill’s methods of agreement, difference and concomitant variation are guides, not proof, when cases are few.
Historical sociology uses chronology, archives and process tracing to explain change over time.
Skocpol explains social revolutions through state crises and agrarian class relations, not class conflict alone.
Tilly ties European state formation to war and extraction; Wallerstein analyses capitalism as a world-system.
Good comparative explanation states mechanisms, scope conditions and rival accounts, and checks selection bias and equifinality.
